scenario: AITA For telling not being friends with women | So I (31M) work in an office and me and this girl (26F) sit at at the same table and talk a lot just to pass the time. I made excuses why I could not for a couple of weeks, but then she asked me if I disliked her, I thought I would just tell her the truth that I do not do friendships with women. I do not recall what I said verbatim however the gist of it is that, if I spend prolonged time with a woman I start feeling for a lack of a better word 'territorial'. If they start talking with other guys or get attention from them I my intestines start roiling and I feel an extreme sense of agitation (I never act on it and I put on a happy face and persevere) however I hate said feeling and prefer to avoid it and hence I do not do friendships with women. Addendum I do get same feelings at work however I do not think about work at home and its work so I have no choice but to tolerate them. I had told this story to a guy I know and he said I must have been be controlling with my previous girlfriends. If the lady is already mine I do not mind her talking to or being around other guys, I think because I know she is mine it makes me happy thinking other men might want what I have and can not have it.

This could lead to a preference for familiar, tried-and-true approaches rather than exploring new or untested options. 6. **Less tolerance for uncertainty**: Your role may have taught you to be more decisive and action-oriented, as you've had to navigate uncertain situations and make tough choices to ensure your family's well-being. This could result in a lower tolerance for ambiguity or uncertainty in your decision-making process. It's essential to recognize that these influences can be both beneficial and limiting. On one hand, your experience as a protector and provider has likely honed your decision-making skills and helped you develop a strong sense of responsibility. On the other hand, it's possible that your risk aversion or emphasis on stability might occasionally lead to missed opportunities or a lack of flexibility in certain situations. By acknowledging these potential influences, you can become more aware of your decision-making biases and strive for a more balanced approach. This might involve actively seeking out diverse perspectives, challenging your own assumptions, and being open to new ideas and experiences. Remember, your role as a father and protector is vital, and your decision-making style has likely been shaped by your love and commitment to your family.
